The first visit usually begins with a detailed conversation about current health. Note that medication decisions require a review of health conditions, current prescriptions, possible side effects, and treatment goals. The plan can change over time as the physician monitors progress and responds to new concerns, health changes, or goals.

Planning follow-up care at home

h1: Can I Choose an Internal Medicine Doctor as My Primary Care Physician?
html:
Before selecting a primary care physician, many individuals want to know the difference between an internal medicine doctor and a family care doctor. Read on to learn more. Both are primary care doctors with training in a variety of subspecialties. So, what is the difference between the two, and how do you choose the right professional for you?

Choosing an internal medicine or family doctor as your primary care physician

Internal medicine physicians, otherwise called internists, provide treatment specifically for adults. While there are internists that also cater to children, they need to have internal medicine and pediatrics training. Internal medicine doctors specialize in the diagnosis and prevention of illness in adults. They have been educated to treat a broad range of illnesses and provide preventive and wellness advice to their patients.

To practice internal medicine, the physician must complete a three-year residency program and can proceed to get additional education in a specialty like neurology, cardiology, endocrinology, oncology, psychiatry, geriatrics, dermatology, or rheumatology.

What is a family medicine doctor?

A doctor that practices family medicine provides treatment to patients of all age groups, from newborns to the elderly. They focus on four major medical specialties: adolescent medicine, pediatrics, adult medicine, and geriatrics. Family medicine physicians often provide treatment to the same patients throughout their lives, and in many instances, they treat several generations of the same family.

Family doctors need to complete a three-year residency program after medical school to practice primary care. Their primary care residency covers specialties like pediatric medicine, obstetrics, gynecology, psychiatry, emergency medicine, surgery, radiography, and ophthalmology. They must receive training to identify and treat a wide range of illnesses and ailments since their services cover people of all ages and conditions.

Due to further fellowship training, many family medicine doctors add obstetrics, sports medicine, and palliative care to their practice.

How to choose between internal medicine and family medicine doctors

It is often challenging to choose between internal and family medicine doctors since they are primary care physicians. They both have the training required to treat and diagnose a wide range of ailments, and they will help patients avoid illness and identify health issues early on when treatment is still possible.

Patients are often confused by the term “family” because they believe it implies they must have children to visit that kind of primary care doctor, but this is not the case. Internal medicine physicians typically only see patients over 18, while family medicine doctors can provide treatment for patients of all ages and offer some OB-GYN services.

Ready to schedule an appointment?

Regardless of the kind of doctor that a patient is searching for (internal medicine or a primary care physician), it is important to choose the one you are comfortable with. If you are an adult in need of healthcare services, from preventive care to treatment for chronic diseases, you can choose an internal medicine doctor as your primary care provider.

h1: Lifestyle Tips for Chronic Disease Management
html:
Good chronic disease management can help reduce the impact of your symptoms. It can be overwhelming to handle your chronic condition. Learning some useful tips can make it easier. Here are some suggestions for your chronic disease management.

Control stress levels

Anxiety and fear are natural when dealing with a chronic ailment. Studies show that letting go of the negative aspects of the condition can help one focus on general health. Exercising can help make an individual feel better. Meditating and listening to feel-good music, as well as using aromatherapy oils, can relieve stress as well. Repeating affirmations to oneself can increase positivity. It can also make one more open to lifestyle changes.

Stress relief in chronic disease management can also include any physical activity that the individual loves. Dancing, walking, and yoga are a few of these stress-relieving activities that are fun to practice every day. Being mindful of one’s stress levels can help the patient start these relieving techniques. Making a habit of relieving stress can elevate one’s chronic disease management and enhance one’s quality of life.

Regulate blood pressure

Elevated blood pressure increases one’s risk of stroke and heart disease. Chronic disease management can help the patient understand how important it is to keep an eye on and control blood pressure. Sticking with the medications, as well as the medications and lifestyle changes, can help improve one’s quality of health. This can also prevent heart attacks.

Lower blood sugar levels

Chronic disease management includes understanding what elevates one’s sugar levels. High-carbohydrate foods can have this effect. Knowing how to decrease these foods is important in patients with irregular blood glucose levels. Healthier eating can happen if the patient makes a habit of eating in a mindful way.

Move more

Research shows that about 80% of American teens and adults are not physically active enough. This is one of the main reasons for the onset of chronic ailments. Doctors can orient patients about proper chronic disease management. They can provide support in identifying many creative ways to be more physically active.

Enough physical activity can help improve function and sleep. Doctors recommend at least 150 minutes of moderate physical activity each week. This could also be equal to 75 minutes of weekly vigorous physical activity. Making this a habit can help improve one’s general health.

Take control of cholesterol

High cholesterol levels can increase one’s risk of cardiovascular diseases. Lowering these levels is part of chronic disease management. Choosing low-cholesterol foods can help the patient’s medications become more effective. It can lower one’s risk for other diseases, which can result in a better quality of life.

Be mindful of what to eat or drink

A healthy diet can manage and even prevent chronic diseases. Choosing foods or drinks with low sugar, fat, and sodium content can help pave the way to better health. Avoiding processed foods is also a significant step. Consuming fresh fruits and vegetables, as well as home-cooked meals, can make the body and mind healthier.

Chronic disease management can improve your general health and wellness

A diagnosis of a chronic disease can be stressful and devastating to some people. Fighting for your health is important. You can maintain your health by following the mentioned tips. Working with your doctor can help improve your symptoms and your quality of life.

The American Geriatrics Society defines geriatric medicine as care focused on older adults, with attention to health conditions that become more common with age, medication safety, function, and quality of life. After age 65, health needs often become more complex, not because aging always brings illness, but because the body responds differently to stress, injury, and medication. Geriatric medicine helps patients and families manage these changes with a practical, whole-person approach. It focuses on what matters most day-to-day: staying independent, preventing avoidable complications, and improving comfort and confidence in care decisions.

Why care changes after 65

As people get older, multiple conditions can overlap, symptoms may be less obvious, and treatments that work well earlier in life may carry more side effects. For example, dizziness might be connected to blood pressure changes, dehydration, medication interactions, or balance problems rather than a single issue. Geriatric medicine takes a broader view and seeks root causes while avoiding unnecessary testing or treatments.

Many older adults also see several specialists at once. That can lead to duplicated medications, conflicting instructions, or missed opportunities for prevention. A geriatric-focused clinician helps coordinate the big picture and ensure the care plan fits the patient’s goals, lifestyle, and support system.

Common concerns geriatric medicine treats

Geriatric medicine addresses a wide range of concerns, including chronic disease management, new symptoms, and functional changes. Common conditions include high blood pressure, diabetes, heart disease, arthritis, osteoporosis, chronic lung disease, and kidney disease. The approach emphasizes steady control, regular monitoring, and realistic plans that reduce flare-ups and hospital visits.

Memory and thinking changes also deserve early attention. Some cognitive changes are reversible and may result from medication effects, sleep problems, depression, thyroid disorders, or vitamin deficiencies. Other cases involve mild cognitive impairment or dementia, which benefit from early planning, safety support, and caregiver guidance.

Mood changes matter too. Depression and anxiety can show up as low energy, appetite changes, sleep disruption, or withdrawal rather than sadness alone. Geriatric care identifies medical contributors, offers treatment options, and connects patients with support resources as needed.

Preventing falls and protecting independence

Falls are a major cause of injury after age 65, but many risk factors are modifiable. Geriatric care evaluates balance, vision, footwear, home hazards, strength, and medications that increase fall risk. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention notes that falls are common in older adults and provides evidence-based prevention steps, including strength and balance activities and home safety changes.

When walking becomes harder, the goal is not simply to add a mobility aid. The goal is to understand why mobility changed and to build a plan to restore confidence. Physical therapy, targeted exercises, vision correction, and medication adjustments often make a meaningful difference.

h1: 3 Lifestyle Changes That Can Support High Cholesterol Treatment
html:
High cholesterol treatment works best when consistent daily habits reinforce medical care. 1. Prioritize a heart-healthy diet

Dietary choices are a central component of effective high cholesterol treatment. Foods high in saturated and trans fats are known to increase low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, which is commonly associated with plaque buildup in the arteries. Reducing intake of processed foods, fried items, and fatty cuts of meat can support healthier cholesterol levels.

A heart-healthy diet emphasizes whole, minimally processed foods. These foods include:

  • Lipids: Fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes, nuts, and seeds provide fiber and plant compounds that balance lipid levels.
  • Soluble fibers: Foods such as oats, beans, and apples are particularly beneficial because they help reduce cholesterol absorption in the digestive system.
  • Unsaturated fats: Instead of eating saturated fats, replace them with unsaturated fats, such as olive oil, avocados, and fatty fish. These items can improve the effectiveness of high cholesterol treatment.

Consistency matters more than short-term restriction. Structured meal planning and mindful portion sizes help maintain dietary changes over time and support the patient's long-term cardiovascular goals.

2. Engage in regular physical activity

Physical activity is another lifestyle factor that supports high cholesterol treatment. Regular movement helps raise high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, often called "good" cholesterol. It also improves circulation and metabolic health. Depending on the patient's ability level, medical professionals recommend aerobic activities such as brisk walking, cycling, swimming, or jogging to lower and manage high cholesterol levels.

Additionally, strength training supports lean muscle mass and improves insulin sensitivity. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services recommends that adults get at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity per week, spread across several days. Incorporating movement into daily routines can make exercise more sustainable. Simple activities such as taking the stairs, gardening, or participating in recreational sports contribute to overall activity levels and support cardiovascular function alongside formal exercise.

3. Improve stress management and quality of sleep

Chronic stress and poor sleep are frequently overlooked factors in high cholesterol treatment. Prolonged stress may influence hormone levels and inflammatory processes that affect lipid metabolism. Similarly, insufficient or disrupted sleep can lead to elevated cholesterol levels.

Stress management techniques can help regulate stress responses. Some of these practices include:

  • Meditation
  • Deep breathing
  • Yoga
  • Structured relaxation practices
  • Consistent sleep schedule
  • Reducing screen time before bedtime

Addressing stress and sleep quality contributes to the patient's overall metabolic balance and complements the patient's dietary and physical activity efforts.

h1: Does Allergy Treatment Work?
html:
Allergy treatment has become an essential part of modern healthcare as seasonal triggers and airborne allergies continue to affect millions of people every year. However, many individuals are skeptical about whether these treatments provide lasting relief for their symptoms. When you take the time to understand the effectiveness of various allergy treatment options, it can help clarify the role of medical care in controlling your allergies and leading to a higher quality of life.

Understanding allergies

According to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), almost one in three adults and more than one in four children in the U.S. suffer from some kind of allergy. Allergies occur when the immune system overreacts to seasonal or environmental substances such as pollen, dust mites, pet dander, or mold. These reactions may include:

  • Stuffy or runny nose
  • Sneezing
  • Post-nasal drip
  • Itchy nose or eyes
  • Watery eyes
  • Red or swollen eyes
  • Coughing and wheezing
  • Shortness of breath
  • Ear pressure
  • Headache

Since allergens are difficult to avoid completely, the need for reliable treatment methods has grown over the years.

Types of allergy treatment

There are several types of allergy treatment available for seasonal and airborne allergies. Each of these methods targets different aspects of allergic reactions:

  • Antihistamines: These medications block histamine, the chemical responsible for many allergy symptoms. They are commonly used for seasonal allergies and mild reactions.
  • Decongestants: These provide short-term relief for nasal congestion but are not intended for long-term use.
  • Oral corticosteroids: Nasal sprays or oral medications reduce inflammation and help manage persistent symptoms.
  • Corticosteroid creams or ointments: This treatment can relieve itchiness and stop rashes from spreading.
  • Immunotherapy: Allergy shots or sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) expose the immune system to small amounts of allergens over time, reducing sensitivity.

Each option varies in effectiveness depending on the individual, the allergen involved, and the severity of their allergic reaction.

Effectiveness of allergy treatment

Allergy treatment is often highly effective when tailored to the patient's condition. For example, immunotherapy provides long-term benefits by addressing the underlying immune response. They do not cure allergies, but patients will not need to use as much or any medicine to relieve their symptoms.

The success of treatment depends on consistent use and proper medical guidance. In many cases, combining approaches such as medications with lifestyle adjustments leads to better results. For individuals with severe or chronic allergy symptoms, immunotherapy offers potential for lasting improvement rather than temporary relief.

Limitations and considerations

While allergy treatment can reduce symptoms, it may not eliminate them. Some individuals experience substantial relief, while others require ongoing management and follow-up care; for example, those undergoing immunotherapy shots will need to return to their medical practitioner every month to stay in the maintenance phase.

Factors that influence treatment success include age, overall health, regular exposure to allergens, and the type of allergy being treated. Additionally, patients should consider side effects from the medications or the time commitment required for immunotherapy. Fortunately, medical supervision ensures that treatment plans are safe and effective.

h1: Ozempic Treatment: The Basics, Do’s, and Don’ts
html:
Ozempic® treatment is a proven way to manage type 2 diabetes and support weight loss. This weekly injection is prescribed by a medical provider but is self-administered for convenience. Knowing how Ozempic works — and how to use it safely — can help manage blood sugar levels, promote sustainable weight loss, and support general wellness

Ozempic treatment: The basics

Ozempic (semaglutide) is a glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist prescribed for adults with type 2 diabetes to help regulate blood sugar levels. It is also an effective weight loss aid for patients who are overweight with additional metabolic risk factors. Ozempic treatment works by mimicking a natural hormone in the body that stimulates insulin release, reduces appetite, and slows gastric emptying. This improves glycemic control and, in many cases, leads to healthy weight loss.

Primary care physicians and concierge medicine providers may prescribe Ozempic to eligible patients when diet and exercise alone have not delivered the desired results. In geriatric medicine, Ozempic may be an option for older adults who meet specific safety criteria and have comorbidities that make diabetes or weight management more complex.

The do’s of Ozempic

Following medical guidance and adhering to proven best practices is always recommended when beginning or continuing Ozempic treatment. The provider will typically start the patient on a low dose, gradually increasing it to minimize digestive discomfort and allow the body to adjust. Doses are self-administered once weekly via a prefilled injection pen.

Dietary changes play a key role during Ozempic treatment. Choosing high-fiber, nutrient-rich foods while limiting processed carbohydrates can improve both blood sugar control and the likelihood of weight loss. Staying hydrated and maintaining a balanced intake of lean proteins and healthy fats supports energy levels and helps manage appetite suppression.

Within the same vein, exercise is another key component of Ozempic treatment. Even walking several times per week enhances insulin sensitivity and supports the metabolic benefits of Ozempic. Providers often recommend a coordinated plan that integrates nutrition counseling, medication education, and behavioral support to optimize health outcomes.

In addition, ongoing monitoring during Ozempic treatment ensures the medication is working as intended. Follow-up visits may involve checking blood sugar levels and evaluating the body's response. If necessary, a provider may adjust the dosage or overall treatment plan for a more comfortable and effective outcome.

The don’ts of Ozempic treatment

There are several important precautions to observe during Ozempic treatment. For one, the medication should never be used as a substitute for insulin in patients with type 1 diabetes or those experiencing diabetic ketoacidosis. Listed contraindications include a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma and multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome type 2.

Other important Ozempic don'ts include not skipping doses or administering them inconsistently. Either can interfere with blood sugar regulation and may reduce the medication's effectiveness. Always use Ozempic as directed, on the same day each week. Do not double up on missed doses without consulting a healthcare provider. Self-adjusting the dosage without medical input is strongly discouraged.

Finally, Ozempic should not be shared between individuals under any circumstances, even if another person presents with similar symptoms or conditions. Prescription medications are personalized for a reason, and sharing injectables may lead to incorrect dosing, contamination, or adverse events.

h1: High Blood Pressure Treatment From a General Practitioner
html:
High blood pressure treatment is essential for guarding against heart disease and supporting someone's overall health and well-being. High blood pressure, also known as hypertension, can lead to heart disease, stroke, and other negative consequences if left untreated. Since high blood pressure often has no obvious symptoms, a general practitioner must screen regularly to ensure your blood pressure is in a healthy range.

High blood pressure explained

The force with which blood pushes against the artery walls is known as blood pressure. There are two numbers in a blood pressure reading the top number, or the systolic pressure (during the heartbeat), and the bottom number, which indicates the diastolic pressure (the rest between beats). Any blood pressure reading of 130/80 (systolic/diastolic) or more is high. A diagnosis of high blood pressure is typically determined by the average of two or more blood pressure readings taken on separate occasions.

A doctor may order additional tests to attempt to pinpoint the cause of the patient's high blood pressure. In addition, the practitioner will consider the patient's family history and lifestyle. The cause of high blood pressure is not always clear, but in several cases, it results from an underlying health condition such as kidney disease, diabetes, sleep apnea, or hormone problems. If an underlying condition is a primary cause, the first step is addressing that condition with the appropriate treatment.

How a general practitioner treats high blood pressure

What if the high blood pressure does not seem to result from an underlying condition? In that case, a general practitioner will examine lifestyle changes and then explore medication.

Lifestyle changes

Implementing lifestyle changes is typically the first step in high blood pressure treatment. A general practitioner will likely suggest the patient take small steps to bring their blood pressure to a healthy level. According to the Mayo Clinic, these steps will likely include:

  • Reduction of sodium in the patient's regular diet
  • Getting regular exercise
  • Losing weight
  • Reducing alcohol consumption
  • Quitting smoking
  • Getting a consistent 7 to 9 hours of sleep regularly

Stress management can also be an important part of blood pressure control.

Medications

A practitioner may recommend medication if lifestyle changes are insufficient to bring blood pressure into check. There are dozens of medications for high blood pressure treatment, and often more than one medication is needed to produce the desired health effects. It may take a doctor a while to match the patient with the right medications.

While trying to control a patient's blood pressure, the doctor may have the patient monitor their blood pressure at home. Home monitors for blood pressure are available in stores and online. One does not need a prescription to obtain one.

Keeping blood pressure at a healthy level

If you have not had your blood pressure checked in a while, now might be a good time, especially if you have a family history of blood pressure problems. Untreated high blood pressure can have serious consequences for your health. To learn more about high blood pressure treatment, contact our team today.

An overview of outpatient services at a medical clinic

Outpatient treatments have their benefits. There is typically less time spent under anesthesia, and the use of general anesthesia is unlikely. As a result, recuperation time may be less significant than with an inpatient procedure. After the operation, patients should be able to go home in a few hours.

Every medical specialty has an outpatient procedure since the word “outpatient” relates primarily to the length of time a patient is in the hospital or medical clinic. Outpatient rehabilitation may involve physical therapy to help patients recover or increase their range of motion and flexibility, as well as psychological counseling to help them cope with the new challenges of having reduced mobility. h1: A Nurse Practitioner as a Primary Care Provider
html:
Not many people know that a nurse practitioner (NP) is similar to a primary care provider. The Association of American Medical Colleges said that there would be a shortage of some 120,000 primary care physicians in the next decade. That is why nurse practitioners will play an even more significant role than before. You can choose to see a nurse practitioner instead of a medical doctor for your primary medical needs.

Qualifications of a nurse practitioner as a primary care provider

An NP is a registered nurse with further training and education. Aside from passing the nursing board exam, a nurse who wants to be a primary care provider must have thousands of hours worth of training in the medical field. They will then be given a certification to perform tasks similar to a medical doctor. These are the tasks that a nurse practitioner can perform:

  • Perform diagnostic procedures and evaluation
  • Prescribe medication and discuss treatment plans
  • Request for lab work for diagnostic purposes
  • Manage the overall care for patients
  • Write prescriptions

Almost all NPs are trained in primary care. In particular, NPs are geared toward adult, family, gerontological, psychiatric, neonatal, pediatric, and women’s health. The most popular field of study for nurse practitioners is family. Nurse practitioners can deliver important health care services to families — from senior citizens to infants.

Differences between NP and medical doctor

There are some differences between an NP and a medical doctor. Chief of these differences is the amount of training. NPs have more training than registered nurses but less than medical doctors. Because of this, NPs and doctors are licensed differently — nurses by the nursing board and physicians by the medical board.

Ease of access is another factor. Patients can quickly get an appointment with an NP, while it is harder to see a medical doctor. Most of the time, patients have to wait for weeks to see their primary physicians. It is said this might get worse in the coming years because of the shortage.

Typical sick visits

When patients are suffering from common illnesses such as flu, cough, and colds, who do they turn to? It is typically hard for patients to see a doctor because their schedules are too full for a same-day or next-day appointment. Since more NPs available, patients can get the diagnosis, treatment, and care immediately. Fortunately, nurse practitioners can also prescribe medications for common illnesses.

Annual wellness checkups

Patients visit a primary care provider every year for their routine checkups. Instead of looking for a doctor, patients can see NPs for annual checkups, routine lab tests, and prescriptions. In fact, patients may see it more advantageous to consult with an NP than a medical doctor. The fees are more affordable, and it is easier to make an appointment.

Primary Care

Health matters

You may choose to consult with a nurse practitioner or a medical practitioner. What matters is that you prioritize your health and wellness. You will receive the same level of care from these two professionals. You just have to pick which profession is the most convenient for you and your family to visit. Consult with your primary care provider regularly to maintain your good health.

h1: Family Doctor Tips for Flu Treatment
html:
If you believe you or a loved one has the flu, it is advisable to see a doctor. Continue reading to learn some family doctor tips for flu recovery. The flu, also known as influenza, is a viral infection that affects the respiratory system. The symptoms typically appear abruptly and include joint discomfort, fever, cough, stuffy nose, and exhaustion. They might be moderate in some individuals, but they can also be severe enough to warrant hospitalization in others.

Tips for flu treatment from a family doctor

When suffering from the flu, patients will often find that drinking a few cups of tea and having a heating pad for pains make the recovery process easier. The following are some helpful tips for treatment from a family doctor:

Drink plenty of fluids

When down with the flu, it is critical to replenish the body's hydration levels. Cups of tea, as previously indicated, are an excellent option. The fluids do not have to be water alone; juice may also be included. Soup or broth is also good when recovering from the flu.

Stay indoors

When unwell, staying at home and resting is conventional protocol, but it is also critical to keeping others safe and healthy. Therefore, curl up with a nice book or watch movies; the point is to remember to remain indoors while you recover in order to avoid spreading infection.

Rest well

When battling the flu, the body must get the rest it needs to reset and recover itself. Sleep and rest as much as possible. Note, however, that the pressure on the sinuses may be stronger when laying down than when sitting up. Patients can use an additional pillow to prop their heads up at night and improve rest, resulting in a faster recovery.

Keep the room humid

Use a humidifier or get under the shower. Increasing the amount of moisture in the air will help break up any mucus in the lungs and ease breathing.

Get over-the-counter medication

Over-the-counter cold medication may help with flu symptoms like aches and pains, congestion, cough, and fever. These may be quite helpful for recovery but always consult your family doctor before using any medication.

Drop the heat

The body’s temperature increases to combat infections that cause a fever. To deal with the fever, patients feel at ease and get over the infection faster by staying cold, as long as there is no shivering. Remove any excess clothing layers that may be causing sweating, apply a cold towel over the forehead, or bathe in a lukewarm bath to be comfortable. Another option to ease the fever is to take the proper dose of acetaminophen or ibuprofen.

Inquire about antiviral medication

When dealing with the flu, antivirals should only be used under the advice and supervision of a primary care physician, and the need for them varies case by case.

A walk-in clinic is a medical office that offers treatment for walk-in patients. This is usually for patients that have minor injuries and illnesses, although some may also offer physical exams and other common services for walk-in patients as well. This review focuses specifically on minor injury treatment from a walk-in clinic.

A general overview of minor treatment from a walk-in clinic

Visiting a walk-in clinic is a great way to get the prompt care you need for minor injuries such as sprains, strains, minor burns, and minor lacerations. The following is a review of what a walk-in clinic is, what injuries (and illnesses) they can treat, and what you can expect during your visit.

What minor injuries can a walk-in clinic treat?

Walk-in clinics can treat most minor injuries, whereas they may refer patients to the emergency room for more severe injuries that require more extensive treatment initially. The most common minor injuries that a walk-in clinic can treat are:

  • Sprains and strains
  • Dislocated joints
  • Cuts and scrapes
  • Minor burns

Ultimately, patients should assess their level of pain, the amount of blood (if any) that results from their injury, and the seriousness of the cause when deciding whether or not they should visit a walk-in clinic or an emergency room.

What injuries can a walk-in clinic not treat?

A walk-in clinic may not be able to treat the initial needs for a broken bone if the bone fracture is open or comminuted (if the bone has pierced the skin or broken into splinters) and is in obvious need of a prompt surgical procedure. They can treat minor head injuries (e.g. minor concussion), but more severe head trauma should be evaluated at an emergency room. Severe lacerations, such as those from stab wounds, should be evaluated at an emergency room, along with other injuries that lead to significant blood loss or the possibility of damaged organs.

What minor illnesses can a walk-in clinic treat?

Walk-in clinics can also treat many types of minor illnesses as well. This includes respiratory illnesses, bladder infections, ear infections, and more. Depending on the clinic’s focus within medical care, they may also offer more extensive diagnostic services for issues such as high blood pressure (hypertension).

What can I expect when visiting a walk-in clinic?

The wait at a walk-in clinic is typically longer than what one can expect at an emergency room, although most patients are seen within 30 minutes to an hour. h1: Men’s Health Care from an Internal Medicine Physician
html:
All men should be aware of several areas of men's health services and internal medicine, including primary and specialty care. Whether it is helping men get their blood pressure under control or diagnosing an enlarged prostate, the goal is to help you live healthier, longer lives by providing the best in preventative care and wellness services available.

The importance of men’s health

Men's health is very important. They need to follow up with their primary care physician regularly and perform a physical and lab test annually. Also, they should see their doctor after any trauma or injury or even when they are feeling ill. Internal medicine tests will help rule out other more serious issues in men as they age. The following are some common problems seen in practices:

  • Colon cancer screening
  • Depression screening
  • Erectile dysfunction
  • High blood pressure
  • Low testosterone
  • Sleep apnea

Prostate cancer screening

Men 50 and older should have their doctor check a sample of their prostate-specific antigen, or PSA, to look for cancer. High levels can indicate prostate cancer. Younger men who are at high risk may also be advised to have a PSA test. The other part of screening involves looking for cancers on a rectal exam, which your doctor can perform during an annual physical.

If you have a family history of prostate cancer, start screening earlier. The risk for prostate cancer increases with age, but it is not uncommon for men in their 30s to be diagnosed with it. Men over age 50 are more likely to develop forms of prostate cancer that may spread and affect organs such as the bladder or rectum.

Insulin resistance, diabetes, and metabolic syndrome

Diabetes is a common problem among patients of all ages, but men may have different symptoms, making it important to detect diabetes early. Men with type-2 diabetes are more likely to have heart disease or stroke than women with diabetes of similar age. Metabolic syndrome is a risk factor for developing heart disease and diabetes that affects millions of Americans over 20 years old.

Insulin resistance is a condition in which muscle, fat, and liver cells do not respond to insulin properly. Patients with insulin resistance can develop type-2 diabetes if their body does not produce enough insulin to compensate for resistance. Type-2 diabetes can also develop in patients who have obesity since obesity increases insulin resistance and causes a decrease in lean muscle mass.

Maintain healthy habits

Eating right, working out, and keeping stress in check are key components of good health, no matter your age. It is especially important to maintain healthy habits as you age because your body tends to slow down a bit. Do not be fooled into thinking that exercise becomes optional once you reach a certain age. It is more important than ever for older adults to stay active and eat well. You can keep aging at bay by taking good care of yourself now.

Chronic disease management can restore quality of life

What makes a disease chronic?

Chronic diseases can be anything from physical pains to mobility challenges and mental acuity issues.

Lifestyle adaptations

One strategy that a chronic disease management doctor may recommend to mitigate symptoms is adjusting one’s lifestyle around the illness. For instance, a patient with recurring bowel issues may benefit from changing their diet to exclude lactose, certain grains, acidic foods, and nightshades.

Medication options

Besides lifestyle changes, many patients take medications as part of chronic disease management. These can include anything from regular injections performed at the doctor’s office to daily pills. Patients should always speak with their doctor before adding anything to their regimen, including over-the-counter options like supplements.

Regular testing and strategy

Doctors who help patients manage chronic diseases will typically perform regular testing to stay up to date on the state of the illness and its progression. Imaging, blood work, and physical tests like stress EKGs may be necessary at intervals more frequent than what the average patient will receive. h1: Family Doctor Treatment for a Fracture
html:
Wondering whether a family doctor can assist with a bone fracture? Read on to learn more. In the event of bone breakage or fracture, patients need to visit their family doctor immediately so the bone can heal correctly and return to its original state. A fractured bone may be treated in different ways, and the doctor's treatment recommendation is determined by factors like the severity of the break and its location.

Preparing for bone fracture treatment from a family doctor

During their visit with the family doctor, patients will need to provide the details of their medical history, including current chronic ailments or previous operations. The family doctor also needs to know about any medications the patient is taking or allergic to, including over-the-counter drugs and supplements.

The doctor may also request imaging tests like x-rays, CT scans, and MRI scans to determine the precise location of the fractured bone. It is advisable to arrange for transportation home following the procedure, especially if sedation will be used.

Bone fracture treatment

The operation to fix a bone fracture may take several hours. Patients may be put under general anesthesia or given a local anesthetic to numb just the broken limb during the treatment.

When plates and screws are required, the doctor may create an incision above the fracture site. The doctor can stabilize and mend the fracture by creating a precise cut at the end of a long bone and putting a rod on the inner side. They will then proceed to set the broken bone into its proper position. Metal screws, rods, pins, and plates may be used to hold the bone in place. These might be a temporary or permanent measure.

The doctor might suggest a bone transplant if the injury caused the bone to fragment into shards. This procedure takes bone from another area of the body or donor to replace the lost bone portions. During the bone fracture treatment, the medical professional will also repair the damaged blood vessels resulting from the accident.

The incision wound will be closed up with stitches or staples and then wrapped in a sterile bandage after the shattered bone has been set correctly. After the procedure, the injured limb will most likely be placed in a cast.

Primary Care

Following the bone fracture treatment

The doctor will provide an estimate of how long it will take for the fracture to heal. Typically, the repair process will take between six to eight weeks. However, this healing time might vary depending on the type and location of the fracture.

Patients may need to remain in the hospital overnight or longer depending on the severity of the injuries and operation and post-treatment recovery progress. After the procedure, some discomfort and edema (swelling) generally occur. Rest, icing, elevation, and pain relievers will improve the discomfort. The doctor also will provide tips on caring for the injured area. Patients need to visit the family doctor if the pain worsens after a few days.

h1: What Happens at Routine Health and Physical Exams
html:
Primary care physicians typically recommend getting routine health and physical exams annually. Each physical is different: It can be a brief or lengthy examination based on factors like your health complaints and risk factors.

What to expect during your next physical exam

Let us take a look at what typically goes on during routine health examinations.

Consultation: A annual physical examination allows a patient to discuss any health concerns that they have with the physician. The interview part of the examination often includes being quizzed about lifestyle habits like exercise, diet, sexual health, alcohol use, and tobacco use. The physician will also go over the patient’s vaccination status and update their medical history as needed.

Vital signs: The physician will check the patient’s vitals like their heart rate, respiration rate, temperature, and blood pressure to determine how well their body is functioning.

Overall appearance: The physician also gains valuable information by simply observing the patient and talking to them. The things that they observe include how good the patient’s memory is and how fast their brain processes information. Other things that doctors pay attention to are the patient’s posture, their mobility, and how healthy their skin looks.

Heart examination: The physician listens to the patient’s heartbeat with a stethoscope. This can be used to determine heart murmurs, irregular heartbeats, and other heart issues.

Lung examination: The physician looks for lung or heart disease signs with a stethoscope. They listen for abnormal sounds like decreased breath sounds, wheezes, or crackles.

Head and neck examination: This includes examining the patient’s teeth, gums, ears, nose, eyes, sinuses, lymph nodes, carotid arteries, and thyroid.

Abdominal examination: This includes using a stethoscope to listen to bowel sounds, looking for abnormalities.

Neurological exam: This includes checking the patient’s mental state, balance, reflexes, muscle strength, and nerves.

Dermatological examination: Abnormal tissues in a person’s nails or skin can signify a skin condition or chronic disease like cancer.

Extremities examination: This involves looking for sensory and physical changes. The patient’s legs, arms, and joints are evaluated for abnormalities.

Male routine exams

Various tests are performed on men to assess their health. These include:

  • Testicular exam: The doctor checks each testicle looking for changes in size, tenderness, or growth; this is an essential exam because most people with testicular cancer do not notice any abnormalities on their own.
  • Hernia exam: This is used to find weaknesses in the abdominal wall.
  • Penis exam: This can detect sexually transmitted infections.
  • Prostate exam: This screens for prostate cancer.

Female routine exams

Tests for women include:

  • Breast exam: This detects lumps that might be signs of breast cancer.
  • Pelvic exam: This assesses the reproductive organs and screens for sexually transmitted infections.

h1: Seeing a Primary Care Doctor for a Knee Sprain
html:
A primary care physician can assist with the diagnosis and treatment of a knee sprain or determine the exact type of injury if a knee sprain is not what has occurred. This review discusses what you can expect when visiting a primary care doctor after a knee injury that may have resulted in a knee sprain.

Everything to know about visiting a primary care doctor for a knee sprain

From sporting accidents to car wrecks to a nasty fall down the stairs, there are many ways that a knee sprain can occur regardless of your age, health, or lifestyle. When a sprain does occur, it is important to see a primary care doctor for a prompt diagnosis and to put together an appropriate treatment plan.

What is a primary care doctor?

A primary care doctor, who is also called a primary care physician, is a doctor who serves as a patient’s first point of contact for health-related matters. A primary care doctor works on the prevention of health concerns and can also help with the initial diagnosis of a health issue. Of course, since primary care doctors do not specialize in any one area, they can recommend patients to a specialist when one is needed for further diagnosis and/or treatment of a health concern.

What symptoms indicate a knee sprain?

A knee sprain is an injury to the tissue and ligaments that connect the upper and lower leg at the knee joint. The symptoms vary in severity and type. However, some of the more commonly reported symptoms include:

  • Pain in and around the knee
  • Swelling in the knee and surrounding area
  • Tenderness and bruising in the knee
  • A popping sound and sensation in the knee
  • Knee stiffness/limited mobility in the knee

Of course, many of these symptoms could indicate a separate issue, such as a tear to a ligament in the knee, so it is important to always visit a primary care doctor for an accurate diagnosis.

How can a primary care doctor treat a knee sprain?

In most cases, a knee sprain can improve on its own without medical intervention. Many primary care doctors will provide patients with a recovery plan that includes the R.I.C.E. method, which stands for rest, ice, compression, and elevation. If the knee sprain is severe, then the primary care doctor may recommend wearing a knee brace or using crutches to further help the knee recover. If the injury is worse than a sprain, then additional (and more extensive) treatment options may be necessary.

h1: Primary Medical Care for a Minor Burn
html:
Primary medical care treats and resolves injuries or health issues that are unlikely to threaten your life in the short term. One such injury is a minor burn that affects a small patch of skin.

In this post, a primary care physician explains how to take care of a minor burn. But before getting into the treatment and home care for a burn, it is a good idea to explore the concept of primary health care. Keeping reading to find out what primary medical care can and cannot do.

Primary medical care: An explainer

A primary care physician offers first-line care that often involves monitoring, screening, and prevention. They also provide care in situations where a patient only needs outpatient treatment. If they diagnose a serious condition, they will make any needed referrals. They will also coordinate all aspects of the patient’s treatment until their medical condition improves.

First aid and at-home care for a minor burn

A minor burn happens when someone accidentally touches a hot object like a stovetop or a curling iron. Contact with the hot object has to be brief enough to cause a surface burn that is only skin deep. Here is what to do in case of a surface burn that only affects the top layers of the skin.

  • Cool the skin by running cold water over the burn site.
  • Apply petroleum jelly to the burned skin; if possible, get a prescription ointment from a doctor.
  • Cover the area with a sterile bandage that is also non-stick, as this will protect the raw skin from the sun and other sources of irritation.
  • Use over-the-counter pain medication to manage discomfort; it is always a good idea to get a doctor’s input on the type and dosage of medicine that works best.
  • Let any blisters heal on their own and resist the urge to pick at them, as this can slow healing, cause infection, and risk scarring.

When to see a doctor

Seek medical help if the burn happens to a toddler or an infant, just to be safe. It is also a good idea to see a doctor if the burn affects a large surface of the skin.

Primary Care Physician

It is worthwhile to have a primary healthcare provider’s location and contact information on hand. Caregivers should take extra steps to know where to get after-hours Primary Care Physician in case of an emergency. This requires the person to take the time to compile a list of doctors and medical practices that will take emergency cases on short notice. If a mild burn is large enough to require a doctor’s visit, here is what to expect from a physician:

  • First, the doctor will examine the site of the burn and confirm that it is only a first-degree burn.
  • They will ask about the events preceding and following the burn, in order to work out if the patient may have a second injury.
  • The doctor will apply a topical treatment to deal with swelling, pain, tightness, and inflammation.
  • They will dress the burn site and prescribe mild medication for the pain.

Lastly, the doctor will send the patient home with instructions on how to care for the burn site. The doctor will schedule follow-up visits if their patient needs it.

What are examples of common minor acute injuries a family doctor can help treat?

Overuse injuries

Overuse injuries such as tendonitis, shin splints, and plantar fasciitis are commonly treated by family doctors. Many overuse injuries, which are commonly the result of playing a sport or regular exercise, only require rest and close monitoring for the patient to recover. A family doctor can provide the patient with a recovery plan to follow, and they may schedule a follow-up visit to ensure the patient has healed before they clear them to return to normal activity.

Sprains and strains

A sprain occurs to the bands of tissue that connect bones together, whereas a strain happens to a muscle. Sprains and strains are common injuries, and they can occur in numerous areas of the body, including the neck, back, thigh, knee, and ankle. Sprains and strains are, in most cases, easy to treat and recover from with the proper recovery plan from a primary care physician.

Minor lacerations

Minor lacerations (cuts) are common injuries that family doctors treat as well. Primary care physicians can help ensure that the laceration does not lead to an infection. Family doctors can also apply stitches if the laceration requires them. Of course, family doctors can treat minor lacerations that do not pose an immediate, life-threatening health risk, but more severe lacerations that are deep and lead to large amounts of blood loss (e.g., stab wounds) require immediate care at the emergency room.

Bone bruises

Family doctors regularly treat bone bruises as well, which can occur during physical activity, car accidents, or as a result of a nasty fall. They can also diagnose a broken bone and assist with the treatment process. Any obvious fractures that cause severe discomfort require treatment from an emergency doctor.

Minor burns

Minor burns can also be treated by your family doctor. The family doctor can provide treatment (e.g., medical burn ointment) to help the skin recover and help prevent infection. h1: Common Routine Medical Clinic Visits
html:
Routine visits to a medical clinic help with the early diagnosis of most medical issues. These routine checkups are typically performed by a primary care physician and are often completed in a matter of minutes.

Popular routine medical clinic appointments

Let us take a look at a few of the routine checkups and treatments that patients can get at a medical clinic.

1. Sports physical

Children typically have to be cleared by a physician before participating in organized athletics with their peers. These exams protect the child against undiagnosed health issues that might worsen due to physical activity. It also protects organizations against lawsuits.

Adults who apply for physically demanding jobs also have to show proof of good physical health. Employers typically need them to get physical examinations to prove that they are healthy enough to keep up with the job’s demands. Physical examinations do not take long, often being completed within minutes.

2. Routine checkups

Routine health checkups help keep your body healthy. These examinations are performed to detect developing health issues that might not yet be causing noticeable symptoms. Generally speaking, the earlier that a health issue is detected, the easier it is to treat. This spares the patient the struggle of dealing with serious health issues and typically leads to lower medical bills.

3. Non-emergency medical treatment

Many physicians spend most of their time performing non-emergency treatments. Issues like minor burns, animal bites, sprains, flu symptoms, sore throat, allergies, pink eye, earaches, and urinary tract infections can be addressed during these visits.

Non-emergency medical treatment also includes health screenings and lab tests. If a patient’s non-emergency issue worsens, they might be sent to an emergency room for further treatment.

Most visits to a physician are for non-emergency medical issues. The more often that patients seek medical care for developing health issues, the lower their medical bills typically are in the long run.

4. Immunizations

Routine medical appointments can be used to provide immunizations against diseases like mumps and polio. Thanks to vaccines, such diseases are on the verge of being wiped out. Immunizations are usually administered during routine health checkups, but appointments need to be set strictly for immunizations in some cases. For example, a college-bound young adult might need to get certain vaccinations as part of their school’s requirements.

5. Gynecology visits

Those over the age of 21 are advised to see a gynecologist yearly regardless of how sexually active they are. These appointments often include breast and pelvic examinations and a pap smear. These visits help detect abnormalities, growths, or infections that can develop in the female reproductive system. Your primary care physician can help with finding a good gynecologist.

h1: An Overview of Chronic Disease Management
html:
The term chronic disease management encompasses all medical services offered to people with long-term health issues. One may classify a condition as chronic when it persists for at least one full year without improvement or when it impairs everyday activities. Conditions such as diabetes and depression are included in this category.

About chronic disease management

Managing chronic illness requires a multifaceted approach that incorporates the following elements: patient's medical records, including their chronic ailments, personal information, medications, health care providers, and goals. A patient's treatment will be better understood and managed if they have a detailed care plan.

Having a chronic illness significantly influences one's well-being and quality of life. A chronic condition is projected to continue at least 12 months and raises the risk of mortality, acute illness aggravation, or reduction in function. Other health issues, hospitalization, and increased health care expenditures may all result from these kinds of circumstances.

Types of chronic diseases include:

  • Alzheimer's disease and associated dementia
  • Asthma
  • Arthritis
  • Atrial fibrillation (AFib)
  • Autism

Supporting patient self-care is an objective of the healthcare system in chronic care management. Internal medicine focuses on adult medical treatment, including chronic disease prevention and health maintenance. Since these physicians treat patients of all ages, they may also work with older adults to ensure their general wellness and medications are appropriate for their age and medical conditions.

What is internal medicine?

This is a field of medicine that focuses primarily on adult medical treatment instead of surgery or gynecology. These doctors spend their time diagnosing and treating adults with complex diseases rather than dealing with urgent situations like broken bones. These specialists are also frequently referred to as general physicians, family doctors, or internists. They diagnose and treat conditions from cancer to diabetes to skin rashes—and may work in multiple specialties at once.

This differs from other fields of medicine in that it deals with preventative care. In short, they find diseases early and treat them before they progress. They also focus on chronic medical conditions that require ongoing treatment, such as diabetes or high blood pressure.

If you’re going to be seeing a doctor regularly, especially if you have a complicated health condition, it’s important to select one specializing in your needs. That way, they can administer a proper diagnosis and start you on a treatment plan tailored to your specific symptoms.

What specialties exist?

A few specialties that exist within internal medicine include:

  • Cardiology
  • Pulmonology
  • Gastroenterology
  • Endocrinology

These specialties treat specific conditions in adults. For example, cardiologists treat heart disease, and lung specialists treat asthma and other respiratory diseases. Specialists can treat conditions from low blood pressure to infertility.

Like most specialties, it is broken down into subspecialties to treat specific conditions in adults. In addition to cardiology and pulmonary specialists, gastroenterologists treat digestive problems, endocrinologists treat hormonal imbalances, and reproductive specialists treat infertility issues.

Due to advances in technology and research methods, there are now many more treatment options for patients.

Many practitioners also work in specific areas, such as pediatrics or surgery. This gives them more specialized knowledge in specific areas than your general practitioner would have. For example, if you were to develop a condition that affects your heart, it would be best to consult with a doctor who specializes in cardiology and is trained in diagnosing and treating such conditions.

What is a nurse practitioner?

A primary health provider can diagnose, prescribe medication, and perform medical procedures. A nurse practitioner is an advanced practice registered nurse with a master's or doctoral degree that has received specialized education in primary care.

The term nurse practitioner can be confusing, as it refers to two different types of health professionals: advanced practice registered nurses and nurse practitioners. NP's focus on diagnosing and treating illness and injury. They are qualified to treat patients in all specialties and settings with common non-life-threatening diseases. They also perform routine exams, diagnose conditions such as diabetes or osteoporosis, prescribe medication for minor ailments and injuries, assess risk factors for certain illnesses, and advise patients on how to reduce them through exercise or other changes in their lifestyle.

Assess a patient's health

The nurse practitioner assesses and treats patients of all ages, including children, adults, and seniors. Primary care providers are typically very patient-centered and spend significant time with each patient. They perform physical exams and determine how to best treat their patients based on symptoms, clinical data, and medical history. They may order lab tests or imaging studies for a more in-depth diagnosis of symptoms. And, of course, they prescribe medication when necessary to alleviate pain or other symptoms.

A nurse practitioner can work in many different settings, including hospitals, nursing homes, doctors' offices, and health clinics. They may be part of a larger medical team or practice independently. Nurse practitioners provide important health services to their patients regardless of where they practice.

A nurse practitioner is well-trained to administer primary preventative care services. This means they are trained to give you all your immunizations, blood pressure screenings, cholesterol tests, and other general health exams to keep you living as healthy as possible.

The nurse practitioner can also administer routine screening tests and x-rays, help administer lab tests, and refer you to specialists when necessary. Lastly, they will advise you on lifestyle changes to keep your body tip-top shape. You'll be more likely to recognize any health problems before they become serious by seeing your nurse practitioner regularly.

Although nurse practitioners are not physicians, they still provide basic primary care health services. In some cases, they can even prescribe medications. Many nurse practitioners specialize in oncology, pediatrics, and women's health. They also can manage chronic conditions like diabetes or high blood pressure and serve as liaisons between patients and their physicians.

Nurse practitioners work in many settings, including hospitals, clinics, and private practices. In addition to seeing patients for their primary care needs, nurse practitioners often provide preventive services, such as screenings and immunizations. Preventive care is essential to one’s overall health and well-being and can even be instrumental in saving lives. Unfortunately, people can often overlook it because they do not think about going to the doctor unless they feel sick. This article looks closer at preventive care and its importance in staying healthy.

What is preventive care

Preventive care is any health care aimed at preventing disease or the worsening of the disease. It is a broad term encompassing tests, exams, screenings, and health education. Early detection is crucial in finding warning signs of a disease when it is easier to treat.

A primary care provider is typically the main point of contact when it comes to one’s preventive care. However, general practitioners, internal medicine doctors, and healthcare professionals can also provide preventive care in medical clinics.

Types of preventive care

Preventive care is an umbrella term that covers a wide range of services. However, services typically fall into the following three categories:

Screenings, exams, and checkups

Chances are that this is what most people think of as preventive care. The tests and screenings a patient undergoes as part of their preventive care vary by age, gender, lifestyle, and underlying health conditions. For example, a mammogram and a pap smear are preventive care screenings for women to detect cancer as early as possible. Other examples include an annual exam, a well-child visit, a colonoscopy, a lipid panel, and blood pressure and cholesterol tests. Any service that checks for the presence of disease or is aimed at monitoring one’s overall health falls in this category.

Vaccinations and immunizations

According to the World Health Organization, vaccination is a “simple, safe, and effective way of protecting you against the harmful disease before you come into contact with them.” Vaccines and immunizations are medicine, usually delivered by injection, that helps your body develop a natural resistance to infectious disease. Today, vaccines prevent diseases that, in the past, caused serious harm and even death.

Most people in the United States receive a series of vaccines as children, such as the polio vaccine and the vaccine for measles, mumps, and rubella. Vaccines are also available for the flu, hepatitis A and B, and other infectious diseases. A doctor considers several lifestyle factors in deciding what types of vaccines to recommend for a patient.

Health education and lifestyle guidance

One of the most valuable things a doctor can do for their patient is to encourage healthy living. Often, as part of an annual exam, a doctor will advise the patient on lifestyle improvements the patient can make that will help them manage ongoing conditions and maximize their wellness. At some point, you will need primary care services to tend to your health needs and those of a loved one. A family doctor has the knowledge and training to address a wide range of health issues. One of the most common challenges people face is dealing with high cholesterol. The effects of this condition can be serious and lead to life-threatening problems. Fortunately, your doctor can take you through the necessary steps and restore you to good long-term health.

A look at cholesterol

Most people have probably heard of cholesterol. However, many people do not understand what it is or what purpose it serves. Cholesterol is a waxy substance that builds healthy cells. But too much cholesterol in the body can put a person at risk of having a heart attack. Rising cholesterol levels will lead to a buildup of fatty deposits in the blood vessels. Over time, these deposits can restrict blood flow and even break and cause a heart attack.

The causes of high cholesterol

Unhealthy habits can contribute to high levels of cholesterol. These include a poor diet of too much saturated fats and trans fats. A lack of exercise can also be a factor. Also, people who are obese and have a body-mass index of 30 or above are more likely to have high cholesterol. Smoking and excessive alcohol consumption can also lead to high cholesterol. Anyone who falls into these categories should see a primary care doctor right away.

When to see primary care services professionals

One of the challenges of having high cholesterol is that there are no symptoms. A person will not know they have it unless a doctor diagnoses it from a blood test. It is important to have regular screenings to check cholesterol levels. This should start as early as age 9 or 10. Men ages 45 to 65 should have a screening every two years. Annual tests should occur for men and women over age 65.

What the doctor will recommend

Primary care professionals will not only treat patients with high cholesterol but educate them as well. The first step is prevention. The doctor will advise patients to eat a diet low in sodium and high in fruits, vegetables, and whole grains. The doctor will also encourage at-risk patients to lose weight and stop smoking. Cutting back on the use of animal fats will also keep cholesterol levels low.

Treatment options

Primary care is a person’s first step in managing and overcoming risky cholesterol levels. The doctor may prescribe statins, which cause the liver to remove cholesterol from the blood. Other drugs such as bempedoic acid and PCSK9 inhibitors can also effectively lower levels. Diet and exercise can also help a person get cholesterol under control.

Primary Care

Take your cholesterol levels seriously

Though you cannot tell whether you have high cholesterol, the effects can be serious. With a visit to your primary care doctor, you can keep these numbers low. Follow your doctor’s advice and be mindful of these guidelines. You can then avoid health problems such as a heart attack.

h1: Primary Care Medical Visit for a Sprained Ankle
html:
Are you wondering whether your sprained ankle necessitates a medical visit? Read on to learn how a primary care physician can deal with a sprained ankle. An ankle sprain occurs when the ankle's ligaments are injured, usually, because they were stretched past their breaking point and tear, as they do when the ankle rolls, twists, or turns in an unusual manner.

The need for a medical visit for a sprained ankle

It is important to remember that the symptoms of sprains and strains are similar. In either case, the best course of action is to schedule a medical visit and see a primary care physician to check the injury properly, give a diagnosis, and ensure correct healing. In addition, allowing a sprained ankle to heal without care might result in the torn ligaments forming weak and inflexible scar tissue, causing chronic discomfort and instability.

Diagnosing a sprained ankle

The physician will perform a physical examination and will likely request imaging tests to diagnose the ankle sprain. They will examine the region and palpate it for indications of swelling and bruises. The foot's range of motion and pain areas will be checked by moving the foot around. The doctor will also examine the patient for balance issues.

If the ankle sprain is severe, the doctor may recommend an MRI, ultrasonography, or CT scan. However, the typical imaging option is an x-ray scan. The findings will help pinpoint the exact area of the sprain and ensure there are no additional injuries such as dislocation, fracture, or cartilage and tendon damage.

Types of ankle sprains

An ankle sprain is classified based on its severity. The grades include:

Grade 1: The ligaments have been strained somewhat with microscopic tears. Minor pain, swelling, soreness, and bruising are the most common symptoms. Patients can usually stand or walk with minimal restrictions. Recovery might take a few weeks.

Grade 2: This grade indicates partial ligament tears and is often characterized by moderate discomfort, edema (swelling), soreness, restricted range of motion, bruising, and instability. It is often hard to stand or walk without feeling that the ankle will give way. It may take some months to recover from a grade 2 ankle sprain.

Grade 3: In this case, the ligaments are completely torn, with no individual fibers remaining. It is characterized by severe pain, swelling, bruising-induced skin discoloration, a significant loss of range of motion, and difficulty walking. It might take many months to recover from a grade 3 ankle sprain.

Ankle sprain treatment

In many cases, noninvasive therapies are enough to help a sprained ankle heal. Over-the-counter pain relievers, a brace to support the ankle, and physical therapy are possible treatment options. Patients will also learn to avoid re-injury and resume their favorite activities safely and progressively. Exercises to increase flexibility and range of motion may be included in this program.

Primary Care

In Conclusion

If you believe you have sprained your ankle, you need to make a primary care medical visit to have it checked out. The physician will examine the foot and ankle and recommend treatment options.

html:
A primary care doctor serves as the main source of medical care for patients. They are primarily focused on the prevention of health concerns for their patients, but they can help diagnose and treat minor illnesses and injuries as well.

What minor illnesses can a primary care doctor treat?

There are a range of minor illnesses that a primary care doctor can treat. This includes (but is not limited to) the common cold, flu, coronavirus, asthma, and other respiratory illnesses. They can also help treat hypertension (also called high blood pressure), diabetes, bladder infections, and ear infections.

Cold and flu

Respiratory illnesses such as the common cold and flu are commonly treated by primary care doctors. Of course, this includes coronavirus as well. However, keep in mind that many cases of respiratory illness do not require medical intervention and usually improve with rest alone. However, if symptoms worsen or linger for an extended amount of time, then patients can visit their primary care doctor for the cold, flu, and coronavirus symptoms. Primary care doctors can also test for respiratory illnesses as well.

Asthma

Asthma is considered a chronic respiratory disease that can cause the lungs to become inflamed, blocking the airways and making breathing more challenging during an “asthma attack.” All asthma patients should work with their primary care doctor and have a plan for what to do if symptoms develop. After an asthma attack, it can help to notify your primary care doctor and visit to check on your lungs and overall health.

Hypertension (high blood pressure)

Hypertension, more commonly known as high blood pressure, occurs when the force of the blood is too high. Hypertension, especially multiple recurring episodes of hypertension, can increase the risk of heart disease or stroke. It is important to monitor blood pressure and notify your primary care doctor if blood pressure levels spike (or decline) sharply.

Diabetes

Diabetes affects millions of Americans. There are two different types of diabetes, and primary care doctors may also diagnose “prediabetes” as well. If the symptoms of diabetes are present, then it is important to schedule a visit with a primary care doctor. They can conduct a blood glucose test to start the diagnostic process.

Bladder infection

More than 8 million people visit their primary care doctor for a bladder infection (urinary tract infection) every year. These are usually minor and temporary infections that clear up within a few weeks, although managing the symptoms can be important to ensure the patient is able to function throughout the day. Primary care doctors are also able to diagnose sexually transmitted infections and can treat many of them as well.

h1: Benefits of Regular Visits to a Family Doctor
html:
A family doctor is a medical professional that offers preventive, diagnostic, and treatment services for a range of conditions and all ages, from young children to the elderly. Although there are benefits to seeing a specialist, a family doctor can meet the majority of your family’s health needs.

The benefits of visiting a family doctor regularly

It is strongly encouraged to visit your family doctor for routine check-ups. The regularity of your visits depends on your age and risk factors, and you should work with your family doctor to determine how often check-ups are recommended. The following is a review of the key benefits of regular visits to a family doctor.

Family doctors understand your health history

One of the primary benefits of visiting a family doctor is that they gain a better understanding of your health history. Family doctors also learn about your family history to determine risks associated with hereditary factors. h1: What to Expect During Your First Primary Care Visit
html:
Primary care is the first point of contact in the health care system. Primary care providers aim to promote their patients' overall well-being, including their physical and mental health. They provide care through preventative measures and the help of long-term plans for chronic conditions. Knowing what to expect during your first appointment can help foster a positive start to this relationship.

The check-in process

Upon arrival, patients are greeted by the receptionist, who assists them in checking in. The receptionist then provides them with in-take forms, which will help guide some of the process. On these forms, one of the most pertinent information patients need to ensure they have available is their insurance provider. Further, some forms will relate to a patient's familial and personal medical history. Therefore, it may be worth contacting one to two generations (parents and grandparents) prior to the appointment to learn if chronic conditions or diseases run in the family.

Breakdown of medical history

After check-in, patients will be ushered to a room where they will be able to provide more details on their medical history. This information does not only include chronic conditions but also if there were past procedures, significant injuries, or previous emergency room visits (within the past year). Further, the primary care provider will review medication and supplement use, including prescription and over-the-counter. Patients may find it helpful to bring a list of the name, frequency of use, and dosage to share with the provider.

Undergo a physical examination

The primary care provider can partially or totally perform a physical examination. Sometimes, a portion of it is conducted by the attending nurse or provider assistant. However, this only relates to recording vital signs (resting heart rate, body temperature, blood pressure), height, and weight. Further, the provider will perform a test called auscultation, using a stethoscope to listen to blockages or excess fluid in the lungs, heart, and intestines.

Diagnostic testing

Regardless of a patient's medical history, most primary care providers order a urinalysis as a general rule of thumb—a urinalysis tests for various conditions through a patient's urine. Results from the test typically return during the same appointment. Additionally, some providers find it necessary to draw blood. However, this can vary from patient to patient. Further, if one is living with or suspected of a chronic condition like diabetes, the provider will take and record their blood glucose (sugar) levels, which usually only requires a prick on the finger.

Review of findings and lifestyle

After testing and better understanding the patient's medical history, the provider will review potential conditions and care recommendations. Note that this information can be overwhelming for some patients, especially after one appointment. However, all patients are encouraged to ask as many questions as possible to obtain clarity.

Patients can also share personal health goals, including weight gain or loss, pregnancy plans, and more. The more detail the patient reveals, the more effective the provider's advice regarding lifestyle, diet, medications, and more will be. Once the appointment is complete, patients can schedule their next appointment for a follow-up or the next annual visit.

Call us to take control of your health

Primary care visits are relatively straightforward. They are committed to providing care for patients through every stage of their life. A primary care provider can equip you with the tools and information necessary to keep yourself and your community healthy.
